gloss: *Ormus*, the ancient Armuza, a town situate on an island near the mouth of the Persian Gulf. It was much celebrated as a mart for pearls and jewels. The form *Ind* (or *Inde*) is common in poets.
“It was the eastern ceremony, at the coronation of their kings, to powder them with gold-dust and seed-pearl” (Warburton); also to strew pearls and jewels at the monarch’s feet.
the Almighty; an obviously fitting title here. Cf. *Tonans* applied to Jupiter.
Moloch (“furious king,” VI. 357) is conspicuous in the great battle in Heaven.

for Milton no word has worse associations than ‘tyranny.’ There is a good deal about “tyrants” and “tyranny” in Milton’s Common-place Book, which reflects his and his age’s deep interest in the question of forms of government.
Milton applies to this nether world terms drawn from the classics. No doubt, M. was influenced by the Renaissance fashion of identifying the Hell of Christian theology with that of classical writers.

used as a noun *drench* (‘that which drenches,’ i.e. wets thoroughly) was, and is, commonly applied to a draught of physic for animals. Here therefore it is a contemptuous word. *forgetful lake* = “oblivious pool,” I. 266.
*proper*, natural = Lat. *proprius*, ‘belonging to oneself.’ Not being subject to the law of gravitation they did not fall, but were driven down by force.
in assigning to Belial the two qualities of personal beauty and persuasive speech M. has followed tradition. *humane*, polished, refined.

words sweet as manna, “the taste of which was like wafers made with honey,” Exod. xvi. 31. *the worse appear The better reason*; alluding, as Bentley noted, to the profession of the Sophists. The reproach was made against Socrates. *dash*, confound, cast down.

*mould*, substance, i.e. of the angels. Spiritual frames, M. has said (I. 117), are formed of an “empyreal substance,” i.e. of pure fire. And this fire, argues Belial, will, through its greater purity, prevail over (i.e. be insensible to) the “baser” fire of Hell.
ironical. *belike*, perhaps, no doubt; only here in M., but many times in Shakespeare. *impotence*, lack of self-restraint (= Lat. *impotentia*).
with all speed.
*rubens dextera* of Jupiter (Horace, *Od.* I. 2. 2, 3).
“He that sitteth in the heavens shall laugh: the Lord shall have them in derision,” Psalm ii. 4. *motions*, proposals, schemes.
editors quote: *Et facere et pati fortia Romanum est*, Livy, II. 12.
*light*, a noun, surely; to take it as an adj., ‘easy,’ is to lose the fine hyperbole that for them darkness may become—light.
his counsel accords with his effeminate character (I. 490). Cf. *Comus*, 759, “Obtruding false rules pranked in reason’s garb.” *ignoble ease* = *ignobile otium*, Vergil, *Georg.* IV. 564.

his speech partly replies to Moloch (since he dismisses the notion of war altogether), partly carries Belial’s counsel a step farther. Belial, type of ease and sloth, stands, as it were, halfway between Moloch and Mammon.

it was a favourite thought with Milton that many men would rather have “Bondage with ease than strenuous liberty” (*S. A.* 271). Aubrey says that Milton’s intense “zeal to the liberty of mankind,” and his republicanism, came largely from his admiration of the Roman writers and Roman Commonwealth.
cf. Psalm xviii. 11, 13; and xcvii. 2, “Clouds and darkness are round about him.”

all existing things were supposed to consist of four elements—fire, air, water, earth; and in each element dwelt certain Spirits or daemons peculiar to it, ruling it, and partaking of its nature. That these daemons were the fallen angels was a common view.
i.e. the “two-handed” sword, “from the armoury of God” (VI. 251, 321), with which in the battle in Heaven Michael laid low the rebellious angels and disabled Satan himself (VI. 320–30).

in Scripture Beel-zebub = Baal-zebub, ‘lord of flies,’ is the Sun-god of the Philistines, his chief oracle being at Ekron, “where answers seem to have been obtained from the hum and motions of flies” (Sayce). In *P. L.* he ranks next to Satan.
worthy of Atlas, one of the Titans, who as a punishment for making war on Zeus was condemned to bear heaven on his shoulders.

there is an allusion to Psalm ii. 9, “Thou shalt break them with a rod of iron.” The distinction between iron typifying hostility and gold typifying benevolence is part of the symbolism in which M. delights.
Addison considered this ancient prophecy in heaven concerning the creation of man a wonderfully imaginative stroke. *fame* = Lat. *fama* in the literal sense ‘report.’
see Gen. xxii. 16, “By myself have I sworn, saith the LORD.” *that shook*; cf. *Aeneid* IX. 106, *annuit et totum nutu tremefecit Olympum*—itself from Homer, *Iliad* I. 530.
originator, parent (i.e. Adam).
often used by Shakespeare of a body of representatives or parliament. So here; cf. the phrase ‘estates of the realm,’ and *états* in French.
*obscure*, obscurity: “palpable obscure” = “palpable darkness,” XII. 188, i.e. “darkness which may be felt,” Exod. x. 21.
i.e. the Universe of this World, hung in Chaos, which is a kind of “sea”: hence the peculiar fitness of comparing Satan, as he journeys through Chaos, to a vessel making for its port (1041–44).

an echo of *Aeneid* VI. 126–29, where the Sibyl tells Aeneas that the descent into Avernus is easy. The slow monosyllabic rhythm and the alliteration seem intended by Milton to suggest the laborious effort of ascent.
i.e. having no substance or being. Night, he means, is a mere vacuity.
anticipated, forestalled.

this simile is typical of many in Milton: similes classical in manner, more like Vergil’s than Shakespeare’s. The peculiarity is that he works the simile out, in all its bearings, into a picture complete in itself but rather detached from the context.
The Civil Wars in England; the Thirty Years’ War in Germany (1618–48); the Civil War of the Fronde in France (1648–52).
trumpets made of the metal called ‘alchemy gold’ or ‘alchemy.’
pass, while away. The picture of the angels variously employed recalls Vergil’s description of the souls of the blessed in Elysium with their diversions, *Aeneid* VI. 640 et seq.
two of the great festivals of Greece were the Olympic games held every fifth year at Olympia, a small plain of Elis, and the Pythian at Delphi in honour of Apollo (the Pythian god).

Hercules, grandson of Alcaeus. Deianira sent a robe dipped in what she thought to be a love-potion: the potion was a poison, and when Hercules put the robe on it ate into his flesh: in his agony he hurled Lichas into the sea, and himself afterwards ascended Mt Œta, raised a pile of wood, and was burnt thereon.
probably M. is ridiculing the theological controversies of his own age: yet he himself discourses on free-will and predestination, not only in *The Christian Doctrine*, but even in *P. L.*
referring primarily to the Stoics: *apathy* signifying in their system insensibility to suffering, hence freedom from passion or feeling.

the chief river of the nether world, round which it flowed “with nine circling streams” (Dryden). *Acheron*, ‘the stream of woe.’ *Cocytus*, ‘wailing.’ *Phlegethon*, ‘flaming’; waves of fire, not water, flowing in its “torrent.”
‘a forgetting.’ “The souls of the departed drank of this river, and thus forgot all they had said or done in the upper world” (Class. Dict.).

Lake Serbonis (now dried up) lay on the coast of Lower Egypt, separated from the sea by a narrow strip of sand; close to Mt Casius. *Damiata*, now Damietta. When Darius Ochus, the Persian, invaded Egypt he lost part of his troops in the lake.

frosty. “This idea of making the pains of Hell consist in cold as well as heat was current in the Middle Ages” (Keightley). Dante makes the last circle, the ninth, of the *Inferno* the frozen circle, where the greatest sinners are confined.
one of the three Gorgons. Her hair being changed into serpents by Athene, her appearance became so terrible that all who looked at her were changed into stone.

for divulging the secrets of Zeus, was “punished in the lower world by being afflicted with a raging thirst, and at the same time placed in the midst of a lake, the waters of which always receded from him as soon as he attempted to drink them” (Class. Dict.).

lemma: Gorgons, and Hydras, and Chimeras dire
gloss: Hesiod mentions three Gorgons, monsters with wings and brazen claws, and hissing serpents, instead of hair, on their heads. The Lernean Hydra was a serpent with nine heads that ravaged the country near Argos. M. mentions these three monsters together because Vergil and Tasso had done the same.
“What simile was ever so vast as this?” (Tennyson). M. had in his mind’s eye a fleet of East Indiamen (Newton).

for Milton’s readers the title *Ethiopian* might more naturally have meant the South Atlantic (or western sea), not the Indian Ocean. *Cape*, of Good Hope. *stemming*, pressing forward, i.e. breasting the waves. *the pole*, the South Pole.

The basis of the allegory of Sin and Death lies, appropriately, in Scripture: “Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death,” James i. 15. In the poem we never meet with them apart.

according to the legend, Circe threw magic herbs into the waters where Scylla bathed, so that she was changed in the way M. implies. *Calabria*, in South Italy. *Trinacria*, Sicily, so called from its triangular shape.
probably Hecate, the goddess of sorcery, is meant. *called*, i.e. invoked to take part in rites.

Lapland was traditionally a home of witchcraft. The belief that the moon and heavenly bodies are affected by magic is very old and widespread. *labouring*; so Lat. *labores* = ‘eclipse,’ *laborare*, ‘to suffer eclipse.’

lemma: the third part of Heaven’s sons
gloss: see Rev. xii. 4. In IX. 141, 142 Satan boasts that his followers were “well nigh half” the angels. Their number was a point of dispute among the Schoolmen.
the comparison of a warrior clad in armour to a comet is at least as old as the *Aeneid* (X. 272, 273). The vast scale of the simile here conveys a profound impression of Satan’s majesty.
a constellation of the northern hemisphere: lit. ‘the Serpent-holder.’ The appearance of a comet was traditionally held an omen, generally of disaster. *horrid hair*, i.e. the tail of the comet.
chosen as typical in poets of a tempestuous region.
by a fitting stroke of allegory, the birth of Sin is made to synchronise with the first sign of disobedience in Heaven.
cf. *Georgic* IV. 525–27, where the river-banks re-echo the name ‘Eurydice.’
lesson, what he had to learn (*lore* and *learn* cognate). Note the change in his tone.
yielding. The phrase is a reminiscence, as Keightley noted, of Horace’s *pete cedentem aera disco* (*Sat.* II. 2. 13). *embalmed*, made fragrant.
as the Son sits at the right hand of the Father (V. 606, VI. 892); profane sarcasm seems intended.
that Sin cannot close the gates is symbolical.
In this picture of Chaos, to be compared with Ovid’s, *Metamorphoses* I. 5–20, Milton labours (as Masson notes) to convey to the reader an impression of the utter confusion of the scene described.
“One would think the deep to be hoary,” Job xli. 32. Perhaps *secrets* = ‘secret places,’ Lat. *secreta*.

“All the ancient naturalists, philosophers, and poets held that Chaos was the first principle of all things; and the poets particularly make Night a Goddess” (Newton). But in personifying Chaos as a distinct divinity Milton seems to have extended the classical conception.
the chief cities of Cyrenaica in northern Africa, a region often treated as typical of sand.

lemma: The womb of Nature and perhaps her grave
gloss: as Nature, i.e. the Universe, was born out of Chaos, so may she at last fall back again into Chaos. He is varying an old thought, that all things proceed from Nature and, perishing, pass back into Nature.

a mythic monster, a sort of chimaera. Cf. Herodotus III. 116, “The story runs, that the one-eyed Arimaspi purloin it from the griffins” (Rawlinson). The legend may have had some connection with the fact that gold is found in the Ural mountains.
i.e. matter now thick, packed close—now thin. The rhythm expresses the difficulty of Satan’s journey.

this picture of the palace of Chaos is as conventional and classical as that of Sin. Such passages owe their similarity to their common origin, viz. Vergil’s account of the realm of Pluto, *Aeneid* VI. 273–81.
a deity supposed to be alluded to by Lucan, *Pharsalia* VI. 744, and said to be first mentioned by name by Lactantius (fourth century A.D.). Spenser makes Demogorgon the lord of Chaos.
by *our* Chaos proclaims himself an ally with Satan against their common foe: their cause is the same.

lemma: If that way be your walk
gloss: Chaos, we see, directs Satan’s course, and wishes him good speed. Yet when Satan, after the Temptation, descends to Hell and announces to his followers the result of his mission (X. 460 et seq.), he pretends that Chaos had “fiercely opposed” his journey.

the vessel in which Jason and the 50 Argonauts sailed to Aea (afterwards called Colchis) to fetch the golden fleece. *Bosporus*, the Thracian Bosporus, now the Straits of Constantinople. At its eastern entrance stood two rocks, the Symplegades; when a ship was passing through they clashed together and crushed it.

the left side of a ship; Ulysses, by steering to the left, nearer to Scylla, thus avoided Charybdis on his right. Scylla and Charybdis were two rocks, close together, in the Straits of Messina between Italy and Sicily.

alluding to Homer’s story of the golden chain of Zeus, suspended from Heaven, whereby he can draw up the gods, and the earth and sea, and the whole universe, though they cannot draw him down (*Iliad* VIII. 18–27).
